lesson_title: The Shortcut That Fails: Compound and Double Angles
hook_text: Everyone wants sine of 45 plus 45 to be sine 45 plus sine 45. Check it with real numbers and watch the shortcut collapse.
clip_script: Here is the tempting shortcut: surely sine of 45 plus 45 is sine 45 plus sine 45. Put numbers on it. Sine of 90 is exactly 1. Sine 45 plus sine 45 is about 1,41. The shortcut overshoots by forty percent. Why? Because angles combine by rotation, not by stacking rulers. Tilt a ramp 45 degrees, then 45 more — the second tilt starts from a slope already leaning, so part of its effort spends itself sideways. The true expansion blends both functions of both angles: sine alpha cos beta plus cos alpha sine beta. Each angle offers its sine, scaled by how upright the other angle leaves things — that is its cosine. And cosine of a sum pairs the functions instead, cos cos minus sine sine, with the sign flipped. Two memory hooks carry all four identities: sine mixes and copies the bracket's sign; cosine pairs and flips it. From these fall the double angles, exact values like sine 15 as a clean surd, and the equations that crack open as quadratics. Never distribute across the bracket. Blend for sine. Pair and flip for cosine.
visual_style: A ramp tilting twice against a protractor, the naive sum bar overshooting a true height marker, then the four identities assembling as interlocking colour-coded tiles.
mood: Myth-busting, punchy, satisfying click at the end.
pacing: A confident wrong claim, an immediate numeric takedown, then rhythmic delivery of the two memory hooks.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and carry all four compound identities with two memory hooks.
